motivation: Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells (2009). In 2012, Park and Snaith independently showed that solid-state perovskite devices could convert sunlight efficiently. Snaith also found that these solution-processed films carry charge over long distances, so the material works as a true thin-film semiconductor. These results opened a new class of semiconductors. Despite being made at low temperature, the materials have sharp absorption edges, low trap densities, defect tolerance and diffusion lengths longer than a micrometre. In about fifteen years, cell efficiencies rose from about 4% to over 26%. Perovskite–silicon tandems have passed 33%, and commercial modules are now being produced. The work has changed our understanding of how disordered, soft ionic lattices can still give excellent optoelectronic properties. It has also produced a technology with clear potential to make solar power cheaper and lower in carbon. This is a discovery of great use to humanity, as Nobel intended.
